title: Linear Inequalities
outcomes: Solve linear inequalities in one variable, applying the sign-reversal rule, and show the solution space on a number line.
Graph linear inequalities in two variables and identify the common (feasible) region of a system, including non-negativity constraints.
Develop inequalities from a descriptive business problem (decision variables, objective, constraints).
Find corner points, evaluate the objective function (including by the extreme-point matrix method) and identify the optimal solution and unused resources.

meta.exam_tip: Optimisation MCQs are fastest by listing the corner points and substituting them in the objective function — never test points inside the region. For "which point is feasible", substitute each option in every constraint.

concepts.title: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
body: An inequality states that one quantity is less than (<), less than or equal to (≤), greater than (>) or greater than or equal to (≥) another. A linear inequality has variables only to the first power.
Rules: adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the sign; multiplying or dividing by a positive number keeps the sign; multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign.

The set of values that satisfy an inequality is its solution space (S.S.). On a number line, a strict inequality (x > 2) is shown with an open circle at 2; an inclusive one (x ≥ 2) with a filled circle.
Double inequalities such as −3 < 2x + 5 ≤ 9 are solved by doing the same operation on all three parts.
concepts.analogy: An inequality is a speed limit — not one exact speed but a whole range that is allowed.
concepts.work: Budgets ("spend at most ₹5 lakh"), capacity ("no more than 2,000 machine hours") and contracts ("at least 500 units a month") are inequalities long before they become numbers in a plan.

concepts.title: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables
body: Step 1: replace the inequality sign by "=" and draw the line, usually through its two intercepts (put x = 0, then y = 0).
Step 2: draw the line solid if the inequality includes equality (≤, ≥) and broken (dashed) if it is strict (<, >).
Step 3: test a point not on the line — the origin is easiest. If it satisfies the inequality, shade the side containing it; otherwise shade the other side.
Standard regions: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 is the first quadrant; y ≤ mx + c lies on and below the line; y ≥ mx + c lies on and above it.
concepts.analogy: The boundary line is a fence; the test point tells you which side of the fence is your garden.
concepts.work: A simple graph shows management at a glance which combinations of output are possible with current resources.

concepts.title: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem
body: Identify the decision variables (what is to be decided — units of each product, bags of each fertiliser) and give each a symbol.
Write each limitation as an inequality: "at most / not more than / available" → ≤; "at least / not less than / minimum" → ≥.
Add the non-negativity constraints x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 — quantities cannot be negative.
Write the objective function — the quantity to be maximised (profit, reach) or minimised (cost, time) — as a linear expression in the variables.
concepts.analogy: Formulation is translation: business English on the left, algebra on the right — the meaning must not change.
concepts.work: Most real errors in planning models come from mis-translating a constraint (≤ instead of ≥, per unit instead of total), not from the arithmetic.

concepts.title: Common region (feasible region) and corner points
body: The region where all the inequalities of a system hold at the same time is the feasible region (solution set). Every point in it is a feasible solution.
A feasible region may be bounded (enclosed on all sides — a polygon) or unbounded (extending without limit). If no point satisfies all constraints, the system is infeasible.

Corner (extreme) points are the vertices of the feasible region. Find them as axis intercepts or by solving two boundary equations simultaneously, then check that the point satisfies all the other constraints.
concepts.analogy: Each constraint cuts away part of a map; what is left after all the cuts is the area you may build on.
concepts.work: Listing corner points is the core of a capacity plan: each corner is a "pure" plan that uses up some resources completely.

concepts.title: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method
body: If a linear objective has an optimum over a feasible region, it is attained at a corner point. So evaluate Z at every corner: the largest value is the maximum, the smallest the minimum.

Matrix (extreme-point) method used in the study material: write the corner points as the rows of a matrix E and the objective coefficients as a column vector C. The product EC lists Z at each corner; pick the largest element for maximisation or the smallest for minimisation.
If the objective line is parallel to an edge on which the optimum lies, every point of that edge is optimal — multiple optimal solutions with the same optimal value.
In an unbounded region a minimum may exist while a maximum does not (or the reverse), depending on the direction of the objective.
concepts.analogy: Pushing a ruler (the objective line) across the region, the last point it touches is always a corner — or a whole edge if the ruler lies flat along it.
concepts.work: Product-mix, diet, transport and advertising-mix decisions in management accounting are solved this way (larger versions use software, but the logic is identical).

concepts.title: Summary of the graphical method and unused resources
body: (1) Formulate: variables, objective, constraints, non-negativity. (2) Graph each constraint and shade the feasible region. (3) Find the corner points. (4) Evaluate the objective at each corner and choose the optimum.

(5) Put the optimal values back into each constraint: the difference between the resource available and the resource used is the unused (idle) resource — useful when deciding whether to sell, rent out or reduce that resource.
concepts.analogy: After choosing the best route, check the fuel gauge — how much of each resource is still in the tank.
concepts.work: Idle-capacity figures feed straight into decisions such as accepting a special order or renting out spare machine time.

illustrations.title: One-variable inequalities
illustrations.q: Solve (a) 3x − 7 ≤ 5x + 1; (b) −3 < 2x + 5 ≤ 9. Show each solution on a number line.

solution.text: (a) 3x − 5x ≤ 1 + 7 → −2x ≤ 8. Divide by −2 and reverse the sign: x ≥ −4. Number line: filled circle at −4, shading to the right.
(b) Subtract 5 from all three parts: −8 < 2x ≤ 4. Divide by 2: −4 < x ≤ 2. Number line: open circle at −4, filled circle at 2, shading between.
Boundary 2x + 3y = 12: x-intercept (6, 0), y-intercept (0, 4). Draw a solid line (≤ includes the line).
Test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 12 is true, so shade the side of the line containing the origin.
If the question adds x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, the region becomes the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 4).

checks.label: test point (0, 0): LHS = 0 ≤ 12, so origin side

illustrations.title: Formulate and solve a product-mix problem
illustrations.q: A workshop makes chairs and tables. A chair needs 2 hours of carpentry and 1 hour of polishing; a table needs 3 hours of carpentry and 2 hours of polishing. Each week 120 carpentry hours and 70 polishing hours are available. Profit is ₹400 per chair and ₹700 per table. How many of each should be made to maximise profit?

solution.text: Let x = chairs, y = tables. Maximise Z = 400x + 700y subject to 2x + 3y ≤ 120 (carpentry), x + 2y ≤ 70 (polishing), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Intercepts: carpentry (60, 0), (0, 40); polishing (70, 0), (0, 35). Both regions contain the origin.
Optimal plan: 30 chairs and 20 tables a week; maximum profit ₹26,000.
(60, 0) uses only 60 polishing hours — 10 hours idle. (0, 40) is not a corner because it breaks the polishing limit (80 > 70).

illustrations.title: A minimisation problem with an unbounded region
illustrations.q: Minimise Z = 6x + 10y subject to x + 2y ≥ 10, 3x + 2y ≥ 18, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

solution.text: Boundaries: x + 2y = 10 through (10, 0) and (0, 5); 3x + 2y = 18 through (6, 0) and (0, 9). Origin fails both, so the region lies away from the origin — unbounded.
Intersection: subtract the equations → 2x = 8 → x = 4, y = 3.
Minimum Z = 54 at x = 4, y = 3. There is no maximum, because the region is unbounded and Z keeps rising.
(0, 5) and (6, 0) are not corners: (0, 5) breaks 3x + 2y ≥ 18 and (6, 0) breaks x + 2y ≥ 10.

illustrations.title: The extreme-point matrix method
illustrations.q: For the workshop in Illustration 3, use the matrix method to find the optimum.

solution.text: E is the 4 × 2 matrix of corner points; C is the column (400, 700) of objective coefficients. Each element of EC is x × 400 + y × 700 for one corner.
The largest element, 26,000, is in the row (30, 20): make 30 chairs and 20 tables.

illustrations.title: Is this plan feasible?
illustrations.q: For the workshop in Illustration 3, are the plans (10, 25) and (20, 30) feasible?

solution.text: A plan must satisfy every constraint (including non-negativity). Failing even one makes it infeasible.

jobs.title: Bakery product mix
jobs.situation: The owner bakes cakes and bread with a limited oven time and flour supply and asks, "How many of each should I bake to earn the most?"
steps: Define x = cakes and y = loaves per day; collect oven minutes and flour per unit and the daily limits.
Write each limit as ≤, add x, y ≥ 0, and write profit per unit as the objective.
Plot, find the corners, evaluate the profit at each, and recommend the best corner.
Report idle oven time or flour at that plan — it shows where extra sales effort could pay.
jobs.takeaway: The graphical method is a practical advisory tool for small clients with two main products.
jobs.think: What would you check if the owner says cakes must be at least 10 a day for regular customers?
jobs.answer: Add x ≥ 10 as a new constraint, redraw the region and recheck the corners — the optimum may move.

jobs.title: Advertising mix within a budget
jobs.role: Finance manager in a consumer company
jobs.situation: TV spots cost ₹50,000 and reach 60,000 viewers each; radio spots cost ₹10,000 and reach 15,000 listeners each. Budget ₹5,00,000; at least 2 TV spots; at most 30 radio spots.
steps: x = TV spots, y = radio spots. Maximise reach Z = 60,000x + 15,000y.
Best: 4 TV and 30 radio spots, reach 6,90,000, spending the whole budget.
jobs.takeaway: Even "soft" marketing decisions can be framed as a small linear programme.
jobs.think: Why is (10, 0) a corner but not optimal?
jobs.answer: It spends the full budget on TV (reach 6,00,000), but moving budget into radio buys reach more cheaply (1.5 per rupee vs 1.2), until the 30-spot radio limit binds at (4, 30).

jobs.title: Idle capacity at the chosen plan
jobs.role: Cost accountant reviewing the workshop plan
jobs.situation: Management chose 30 chairs and 20 tables (Illustration 3). The plant head asks whether any carpentry or polishing hours will be idle.
steps: Both resources are binding — any increase in output needs more of both.
Compare with the plan (60, 0): carpentry idle 0, polishing idle 10 hours.
jobs.takeaway: At an intersection corner both constraints are binding; at an axis corner some resource is often idle.
jobs.think: If 10 more polishing hours could be hired, would the optimum change?
jobs.answer: Yes — the polishing line moves outward, the intersection corner shifts, and the new corner must be re-evaluated.

mcqs.q: The solution of 4x − 3 > 2x + 7 is:
mcqs.explain: Move terms: 4x − 2x > 7 + 3, so 2x > 10 and x > 5. Dividing by a positive number (2) keeps the sign the same. The trap is x ≥ 5, which wrongly includes 5 — at x = 5 both sides equal 17, so the strict '>' fails. In practice: a strict inequality such as 'sales must exceed ₹5 lakh to earn a bonus' means exactly ₹5 lakh does not qualify, a distinction HR and payroll teams must apply carefully.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: The solution of −2x + 5 ≤ 11 is:
mcqs.explain: Subtract 5: −2x ≤ 6. Dividing by −2 reverses the sign, giving x ≥ −3. Check: x = −3 gives 11 ≤ 11 (true) and x = −4 gives 13 ≤ 11 (false). The trap is x ≤ −3, which divides by −2 but forgets to flip the sign. In practice: rearranging constraints that contain negative coefficients — for example a cost limit written in terms of savings — needs this sign flip, or the allowed range ends up exactly backwards.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: When both sides of an inequality are multiplied by a negative number:
mcqs.explain: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality: from 3 > 2 we get −3 < −2. The tempting wrong belief is that the sign stays unchanged, which is true only for positive multipliers or for adding and subtracting any number. In practice: when an analyst converts a 'loss must not exceed ₹2 lakh' condition into a profit condition (multiplying by −1), the direction of the sign flips.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: The solution of −1 ≤ (3x − 2)/4 < 2 is:
mcqs.explain: Multiply all three parts by 4: −4 ≤ 3x − 2 < 8. Add 2: −2 ≤ 3x < 10. Divide by 3: −2/3 ≤ x < 10/3. The trap is −2/3 < x ≤ 10/3, which has the right numbers but swaps which end is included — the ≤ stays with the left end and the < with the right. In practice: a double inequality describes a band, such as a tolerance range for a product's weight, and the included ends matter when an auditor tests compliance.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: While graphing 3x + 2y < 12, the line 3x + 2y = 12 is drawn:
options: As a broken (dashed) line, because points on it are excluded
mcqs.explain: A strict inequality (< or >) excludes points on the boundary, so the line 3x + 2y = 12 is drawn broken (dashed) to show it is not part of the region. The trap is 'as a solid line', which is used only for ≤ or ≥ where the boundary is included. In practice: in a production graph, a dashed boundary tells the manager that working exactly at that capacity limit is not allowed — a detail that matters when reading feasible output plans.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: The region represented by 2x + 5y ≤ 10 is:
options: The side of the line 2x + 5y = 10 that contains the origin, including the line
The side away from the origin
mcqs.explain: Draw the line 2x + 5y = 10 and test the origin: 2(0) + 5(0) = 0 ≤ 10 is true, so the region is the side containing the origin, and the line itself is included because of '≤'. The trap is 'the side away from the origin', which would be correct for ≥. In practice: resource limits like 'machine hours used ≤ hours available' always give the origin side, since producing nothing uses nothing.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: Which point satisfies both x + y ≤ 6 and x − y ≥ 2?
mcqs.explain: Test each point in both inequalities. (4, 1): 4 + 1 = 5 ≤ 6 and 4 − 1 = 3 ≥ 2 — both hold, so it is in the common region. The trap is (1, 4), which reverses the coordinates and gives 1 − 4 = −3, failing x − y ≥ 2; (6, 2) gives 8, failing the first. In practice: before accepting a proposed production plan, a cost accountant substitutes it into every constraint — failing even one makes it infeasible.
mcqs.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points

mcqs.q: The inequalities x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 together represent:
options: The first quadrant including the axes
mcqs.explain: x ≥ 0 keeps points on or to the right of the y-axis and y ≥ 0 keeps points on or above the x-axis. Together they give the first quadrant, including both axes. The trap is 'only the origin', which would need x = 0 and y = 0 rather than ≥. In practice: these are the non-negativity conditions of every linear programming problem, since a factory cannot make a negative number of units.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: The region x ≤ 0, y ≥ 0 lies in the:
mcqs.explain: x ≤ 0 means points on or to the left of the y-axis; y ≥ 0 means on or above the x-axis. The region where x is negative (or zero) and y is positive (or zero) is the second quadrant. The trap is the fourth quadrant, which reverses the signs (x positive, y negative). In practice: reading quadrants correctly matters when plotting profit against change in price, where negative values represent price cuts.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: The line 4x + 3y = 24 cuts the axes at:
mcqs.explain: To find intercepts, put one variable to zero. With y = 0, 4x = 24 and x = 6; with x = 0, 3y = 24 and y = 8. So the line cuts the axes at (6, 0) and (0, 8). The trap is (8, 0) and (0, 6), which swaps the intercepts by dividing by the wrong coefficient. In practice: these intercepts show the maximum of each product if the whole resource went to it alone — a quick capacity check in product-mix planning.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The maximum value is:
mcqs.explain: The feasible region has corners (0, 0), (5, 0) and (0, 5). Evaluate Z = 3x + 2y: 0, 15 and 10. The maximum is 15 at (5, 0). The trap is 10, the value at (0, 5) — picking the corner with the smaller coefficient. Another trap is 25, which adds 3 + 2 and multiplies by 5 as if both could be 5 at once. In practice: a firm with one shared resource puts it all into the product with the higher contribution per unit of that resource.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: Maximise Z = 2x + 3y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x + 3y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0. The maximum value is:
mcqs.explain: Corners are (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 2) and the intersection of x + y = 4 and x + 3y = 6, which is (3, 1). Z = 2x + 3y gives 0, 8, 6 and 9, so the maximum is 9 at (3, 1). The trap is 8 at (4, 0), from checking only the axis corners and missing the intersection point. In practice: the best product mix often lies where two resource limits bind together, which is why the intersection corner must always be tested.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: Minimise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x + y ≥ 4, x + 3y ≥ 6, x, y ≥ 0. The minimum value is:
mcqs.explain: With ≥ constraints the region is unbounded, with corners (0, 4), (3, 1) and (6, 0). Z = 3x + 5y gives 20, 14 and 18, so the minimum cost is 14 at (3, 1). The trap is 18, from testing only the axis corners and missing the intersection; 10 is not attainable at any feasible point. In practice: diet-mix and blending problems, like choosing cattle feed or fertiliser at least cost, are solved exactly this way.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: If an optimal solution exists, it occurs:
options: At a corner (extreme) point of the feasible region
At the centre of the feasible region
mcqs.explain: For a linear objective over a feasible region bounded by straight lines, the optimum (if it exists) is reached at a corner (extreme) point; that is why we evaluate only the corners. The trap is 'at the centre of the feasible region' — moving from the centre towards an edge always improves a linear objective. In practice: this corner-point principle underlies the software that refiners, airlines and FMCG planners use to optimise production and logistics.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: If the objective function line is parallel to an edge of the feasible region along which the optimum lies:
options: There are multiple optimal solutions with the same optimal value
The optimum is at the origin
mcqs.explain: If the objective line is parallel to an edge where the optimum lies, every point on that edge gives the same best value, so there are multiple (infinitely many) optimal solutions. The trap is 'there is no solution' — the problem is perfectly solvable, it just has many equally good answers. In practice: multiple optima give management flexibility to choose the plan that is best on non-financial grounds, such as smoother staffing or customer commitments.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: A feasible region that is not enclosed on all sides is called:
mcqs.explain: A feasible region that extends indefinitely in some direction is called unbounded. In such a region a maximum may not exist, although a minimum often does. The trap is 'infeasible', which means there is no common region at all — the opposite situation. In practice: cost-minimisation problems with 'at least' requirements, like minimum nutrient or minimum output targets, usually have unbounded regions.
mcqs.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points

mcqs.q: Shirts need 2 hours and trousers 3 hours of tailoring; at most 60 hours are available. With x shirts and y trousers:
mcqs.explain: Each shirt uses 2 hours and each pair of trousers 3 hours, so x shirts and y trousers use 2x + 3y hours, which cannot exceed 60: 2x + 3y ≤ 60. The trap is 3x + 2y ≤ 60, which attaches the hours to the wrong product; '≥' would turn a capacity limit into a minimum. In practice: a garment unit's planner writes one such constraint for each department — cutting, stitching, finishing — before choosing a product mix.
mcqs.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem

mcqs.q: Food P gives 4 units of protein per kg and food Q gives 5 units. A diet needs at least 20 units. The constraint is:
mcqs.explain: x kg of P supplies 4x units and y kg of Q supplies 5y units of protein, and 'at least 20 units' means the total must be 20 or more: 4x + 5y ≥ 20. The trap is 4x + 5y ≤ 20, which turns a minimum requirement into a maximum. In practice: nutrition planners for midday-meal schemes and cattle-feed makers write minimum-requirement constraints like this before finding the cheapest mix.
mcqs.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem

mcqs.q: Non-negativity constraints state that:
mcqs.explain: Non-negativity constraints state that the decision variables cannot be negative: x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Zero is allowed, because a firm may choose not to make one of the products. The trap is x > 0 and y > 0, which wrongly rules out zero production. In practice: in a product-mix plan the optimal answer may well be to drop a product entirely, so zero must remain allowed.
mcqs.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem

mcqs.q: The region 3x − 4y ≥ 12 is:
options: The side of the line not containing the origin
mcqs.explain: Test the origin: 3(0) − 4(0) = 0, and 0 ≥ 12 is false, so the origin is not in the region. The region is the side of the line 3x − 4y = 12 away from the origin (with the line included). The trap is 'the side containing the origin', which applies when the origin satisfies the inequality. In practice: minimum-output requirements give regions away from the origin, since producing nothing cannot meet them.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: How many integers satisfy both 2x − 3 > 0 and x < 5?
mcqs.explain: 2x − 3 > 0 gives x > 1.5, and the second condition is x < 5. The integers strictly between 1.5 and 5 are 2, 3 and 4 — three integers. The trap is 4, which wrongly includes 5 (or 1) by ignoring that both inequalities are strict. In practice: counting whole units within a range — such as the number of batch sizes that satisfy two capacity limits — needs care at both ends.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: How many integers satisfy −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7?
mcqs.explain: Subtract 1 throughout: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integers are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2 — five integers. The trap is 6, which wrongly includes 3 even though the right-hand inequality is strict. In practice: such ranges describe slabs and bands — for example, income brackets in a tax table — where one end is included and the other is not.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: The region x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x ≤ 4, y ≤ 5, x + y ≤ 7 has corner points (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3), (2, 5), (0, 5). The maximum of Z = x + 2y is:
mcqs.explain: Evaluate Z = x + 2y at each corner: (0, 0) → 0, (4, 0) → 4, (4, 3) → 10, (2, 5) → 12, (0, 5) → 10. The maximum is 12 at (2, 5). The trap is 10, the tied value at (4, 3) and (0, 5), from stopping before checking every corner. In practice: in product-mix decisions, evaluating every corner — not just the obvious ones — is what ensures the plan with the highest contribution is not missed.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: At the point (3, 2), how much of the resource in the constraint 2x + y ≤ 10 is left unused?
mcqs.explain: Resource used at (3, 2) = 2(3) + 2 = 8 units out of the 10 available, so 10 − 8 = 2 units remain unused (the slack). The trap is 8, which is the amount used, not the amount left. In practice: slack shows idle capacity — for example spare machine hours — that management can redeploy, rent out or use for a new order.
mcqs.topic: Summary of the graphical method and unused resources

mcqs.q: The region y ≥ x + 2 consists of points:
options: On and above the line y = x + 2
To the right of the line only
mcqs.explain: y ≥ x + 2 means that for each x, y must be at least x + 2, so the region consists of points on the line y = x + 2 and above it. The trap is 'below the line only', which describes y < x + 2. In practice: a pricing rule like 'selling price must be at least cost plus ₹2' gives exactly this kind of region, on and above the cost-plus line.
mcqs.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a linear inequality?
mcqs.explain: A linear inequality has each variable only to the power 1. In x² + y ≤ 4, the x² term makes it non-linear (its boundary is a parabola, not a straight line). The tempting wrong choice is x ≥ 0, which looks too simple to count, but it is a valid linear inequality in one variable. In practice: linear programming tools need linear constraints, so an analyst must spot squared or product terms before choosing a method.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: On a number line, x > 2 is shown by:
options: An open (hollow) circle at 2 with shading to the right
A filled circle at 2 with shading to the right
An open circle at 2 with shading to the left
mcqs.explain: x > 2 excludes 2 itself, so it is shown by an open (hollow) circle at 2 with shading to the right for all larger values. The trap is a filled circle at 2, which would mean x ≥ 2, including 2. In practice: on a chart of eligibility thresholds — for example 'turnover above ₹2 crore' — the open circle signals that the exact threshold value does not qualify.
mcqs.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space

mcqs.q: Using the matrix method, the extreme points (0, 0), (5, 0), (2, 3), (0, 4) are multiplied by the objective column (3, 4) for Z = 3x + 4y. The maximum element of EC is:
mcqs.explain: Multiply each extreme point by the objective column (3, 4): (0, 0) → 0, (5, 0) → 15, (2, 3) → 6 + 12 = 18, (0, 4) → 16. EC = (0, 15, 18, 16), and the maximum element is 18 at (2, 3). The trap is 16 at (0, 4), which favours the larger coefficient but ignores the mixed corner. In practice: the matrix method is just an organised table for evaluating all corners, the same way a spreadsheet tests options in parallel.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

questions.q: Find the corner points of the region 2x + y ≤ 10, x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, and find the maximum of Z = 3x + 4y over it.

model.text: Intercepts: 2x + y = 10 → (5, 0), (0, 10); x + 2y = 8 → (8, 0), (0, 4). Origin satisfies both, so the region is towards the origin.
Intersection: double the second equation: 2x + 4y = 16; subtract the first: 3y = 6 → y = 2, x = 4.

scheme.pt: Correct intercepts and side of each line
Evaluates Z and states the maximum

remarks: Including (8, 0) or (0, 10) as corners is the classic error — they violate the other constraint.
mistakes: Not checking each candidate corner against all constraints.
Evaluating Z at the intercepts of only one line.
tips: Put the corners and Z values in a two-column table — quick to mark and to check.

checks.label: y at intersection of 2x + y = 10 and x + 2y = 8

questions.q: A firm makes products P and Q. P needs 1 machine hour and 2 labour hours; Q needs 2 machine hours and 1 labour hour. 40 machine hours and 50 labour hours are available. Profit is ₹30 per unit of P and ₹20 per unit of Q. Formulate and solve graphically.

model.text: Let x, y be units of P and Q. Maximise Z = 30x + 20y subject to x + 2y ≤ 40, 2x + y ≤ 50, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Intercepts: machine (40, 0), (0, 20); labour (25, 0), (0, 50). Intersection: x = 40 − 2y → 80 − 4y + y = 50 → y = 10, x = 20.
Make 20 units of P and 10 of Q; maximum profit ₹800.

scheme.pt: Correct objective and constraints with non-negativity

remarks: Swapping the coefficients (writing 2x + y ≤ 40 for machine hours) is the commonest formulation error.
mistakes: Choosing (40, 0) which breaks the labour constraint.
tips: Make a small data table (product × resource) before writing constraints.

questions.q: Minimise Z = 20x + 30y subject to x + y ≥ 6, x + 3y ≥ 12, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Comment on the existence of a maximum.

model.text: Lines: x + y = 6 through (6, 0), (0, 6); x + 3y = 12 through (12, 0), (0, 4). The origin fails both, so the region lies away from it and is unbounded.
Minimum Z = 150 at (3, 3). No maximum exists because the region is unbounded and Z increases without limit.

remarks: Many candidates use (0, 4) or (6, 0) as corners — both fail the other constraint.
mistakes: Shading towards the origin for ≥ constraints.
Stating a maximum for an unbounded region.
tips: Always test the origin for each constraint and write the result in one line.

summary: Adding/subtracting keeps the sign; multiplying/dividing by a negative reverses it.
Open circle for < or >, filled circle for ≤ or ≥ on a number line.
Graph: draw the boundary (solid for ≤/≥, broken for </>), test the origin, shade the correct side.
Feasible region = common region of all constraints including x, y ≥ 0; bounded or unbounded.
Optimum occurs at a corner point; evaluate Z at all corners (or use EC in the matrix method).
Objective parallel to an optimal edge → multiple optimal solutions with the same value.
Unused resource = available − used at the optimal point.
remember: "At most / not more than / available" → ≤; "at least / minimum" → ≥.
A candidate corner must satisfy every constraint.
Unbounded region: a minimum may exist with no maximum.
traps: Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative.
Taking axis intercepts that violate another constraint as corners.
Testing interior points instead of corners.

viva.q: What happens to an inequality when you add a number to both sides, and when you multiply both sides by a negative number?
viva.model: Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides does not change the inequality sign. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number also keeps the sign, but multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality.

viva.q: What is a feasible region in a system of linear inequalities?
viva.model: The feasible region is the common region where all the constraints, including the non-negativity constraints, are satisfied at the same time. Every point inside it or on its boundary is a feasible solution. It can be bounded, like a closed polygon, or unbounded.

viva.q: Where does the optimal solution of a linear programme lie, and how do you find it graphically?

viva.q: When does a linear programme have multiple optimal solutions?
viva.model: When the objective function line is parallel to an edge, or side, of the feasible region on which the optimum lies. Then every point on that edge gives the same optimal value, so there are many optimal solutions but only one optimal value.

cases.title: Cheapest fertiliser mix for a farm client
cases.case: Shakti Agro must supply at least 9 kg of nitrogen (N) and 8 kg of phosphate (P) to a field. Fertiliser A contains 3 kg N and 1 kg P per bag and costs ₹500 a bag. Fertiliser B contains 1 kg N and 2 kg P per bag and costs ₹400 a bag. Let x and y be the bags of A and B bought. The aim is to meet both requirements at the lowest cost.

mcqs.q: The nitrogen requirement is written as:
mcqs.explain: Each bag of A gives 3 kg of nitrogen and each bag of B gives 1 kg, so x bags of A and y of B supply 3x + y kg. 'At least 9 kg' means 3x + y ≥ 9. The trap is x + 2y ≥ 9, which uses the phosphate contents instead of nitrogen; ≤ would turn the minimum into a maximum. In practice: agronomists and agri-input firms set up exactly such nutrient constraints from soil-test reports before recommending a fertiliser mix.
mcqs.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem

mcqs.q: The two requirement lines 3x + y = 9 and x + 2y = 8 meet at:
mcqs.explain: From 3x + y = 9, y = 9 − 3x. Substitute in x + 2y = 8: x + 18 − 6x = 8, so x = 2 and y = 3. Check: 3(2) + 3 = 9 and 2 + 2(3) = 8. The trap is (3, 2), which swaps the coordinates and satisfies neither line. In practice: this intersection is the corner where both nutrient requirements are met exactly, with no wasted fertiliser — typically where the cheapest mix lies.
mcqs.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points

mcqs.q: The minimum cost is:
mcqs.explain: The region is unbounded with corners (0, 9), (2, 3) and (8, 0). Cost = 500x + 400y gives ₹3,600, ₹2,200 and ₹4,000, so the minimum is ₹2,200 with 2 bags of A and 3 of B. The trap is ₹3,600, from buying only fertiliser B because each bag is cheaper. In practice: the cheapest per-bag product is rarely the cheapest way to meet several requirements — farm advisers and procurement teams compare cost per requirement met.
mcqs.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method

mcqs.q: If the farm buys only fertiliser A (the corner (8, 0)), how much nitrogen is supplied in excess of the requirement?
mcqs.explain: Eight bags of A supply 8 × 3 = 24 kg of nitrogen, but only 9 kg is required, so the excess (surplus) is 24 − 9 = 15 kg. The trap is 24 kg, which is the total supplied, not the excess over the requirement. In practice: surplus nutrients are paid for but wasted, which is why a cost accountant reports surplus alongside cost when comparing input plans.
mcqs.topic: Summary of the graphical method and unused resources

mcqs.q: Why can we not find a maximum cost for this problem?
options: The objective function is not linear
mcqs.explain: With 'at least' (≥) constraints, the feasible region stretches away indefinitely: buying more bags always satisfies the requirements, so cost can rise without limit. The region is unbounded, so only a minimum cost exists. The trap is 'the constraints are inconsistent' — they are consistent, since a feasible region clearly exists. In practice: a cost-minimisation problem never asks for the 'maximum cost', because a buyer can always overspend.
mcqs.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points
